title: I. They Arrive At The Monastery
paragraphs: It was a warm, bright day at the end of August. The meeting with the elder had been set for half-past eleven, right after late mass. Our visitors didn't attend the service, but arrived just as it was ending. First, an elegant open carriage, drawn by two fine horses, pulled up carrying Miüsov and a distant relative of his, a young man of twenty named Pyotr Fomitch Kalganov. This young man was preparing to enter university. Miüsov, with whom he was staying at the time, was trying to talk him into going abroad to study at Zurich or Jena. The young man was still undecided. He was pensive and absent-minded. He was nice-looking, sturdily built, and rather tall. There was an odd fixed quality to his gaze at times. Like all very absent-minded people, he'd sometimes stare straight at someone without actually seeing them. He was quiet and rather awkward, but sometimes, alone with someone, he'd turn talkative and animated, laughing at anything or nothing at all. But his liveliness would vanish as quickly as it appeared. He was always dressed well, even elaborately; he already had some money of his own, with expectations of a good deal more. He was a friend of Alyosha's.

In an ancient, jolting but roomy hired carriage, drawn by a pair of old pinkish-gray horses, a good way behind Miüsov's, came Fyodor Pavlovitch with his son Ivan. Dmitri was late, though he'd been told the time the evening before. The visitors left their carriages at the hotel, outside the grounds, and walked to the monastery gates on foot. Except for Fyodor Pavlovitch, none of the party had ever seen the monastery before, and Miüsov had probably not set foot in a church in thirty years. He looked around with curiosity, along with a certain studied ease. But apart from the church and the outbuildings—ordinary enough in themselves—he found nothing of interest inside the monastery grounds. The last worshippers were coming out of the church, bareheaded, crossing themselves. Among the humbler people were a few of higher rank—two or three ladies and a very old general, all staying at the hotel. Our visitors were immediately surrounded by beggars, but none of them gave anything, except young Kalganov, who took a ten-copeck piece from his purse and, nervous and flustered—God knows why—hurriedly handed it to an old woman, saying, “Share it out equally.” None of his companions made any remark about it, so he had no real reason to be embarrassed, but, noticing this, he was even more thrown off.

It was odd that their arrival didn't seem to have been expected, and that they weren't received with any particular honor, even though one of them had recently made a donation of a thousand roubles, while another was an extremely wealthy, highly cultured landowner on whom, in a sense, the whole monastery depended, since a ruling in his lawsuit could put their fishing rights in his hands at any moment. Yet no official of the monastery came out to meet them.

Miüsov glanced absently at the tombstones around the church, and was on the verge of remarking that the dead buried here must have paid a pretty penny for the right to lie in this “holy place,” but held his tongue. His liberal irony was rapidly curdling into something closer to anger.
“Who the devil is there to ask, in this idiotic place? We need to find out, time's getting on,” he muttered, as though talking to himself.

All at once a bald, elderly man with fawning little eyes came up, wearing a long summer overcoat. Lifting his hat, he introduced himself with a honeyed lisp as Maximov, a landowner from Tula. He at once got wind of our visitors' difficulty.
“Father Zossima lives in the hermitage, off by itself, four hundred paces from the monastery, on the other side of the copse.”
“I know it's the other side of the copse,” said Fyodor Pavlovitch, “but we don't remember the way. It's been a long time since we were here.”
“This way, through this gate, straight across the copse… the copse. Come with me, won't you? I'll show you. I have to go… I'm going myself. This way, this way.”

They came out through the gate and turned toward the copse. Maximov, a man of sixty, ran rather than walked, turning sideways to stare at them all with an almost incredible degree of nervous curiosity, his eyes seeming to bulge out of his head.

“You see, we've come to the elder on business of our own,” Miüsov observed sternly. “That personage has granted us an audience, so to speak, and so, though we thank you for showing us the way, we can't ask you to come along with us.”
“I've already been there. I've been already; _un chevalier parfait_,” and Maximov snapped his fingers in the air.
“Who's a _chevalier_?” asked Miüsov.
“The elder, the splendid elder, the elder! The honor and glory of the monastery. Zossima. What an elder!”
But his rambling chatter was cut off by a very pale, wan-looking monk of medium height, wearing a monk's cap, who caught up with them. Fyodor Pavlovitch and Miüsov stopped.
The monk, with an extremely courteous, deep bow, announced:
“The Father Superior invites all of you, gentlemen, to dine with him after your visit to the hermitage. At one o'clock, no later.” And to Maximov: “And you as well.”

“That I certainly will, without fail,” cried Fyodor Pavlovitch, hugely pleased by the invitation. “And, believe me, we've all given our word to behave ourselves here… And you, Pyotr Alexandrovitch, will you go too?”
“Yes, of course. What did I come for, if not to study every custom here? The only thing standing in my way is your company…”
“Yes—Dmitri Fyodorovitch doesn't exist yet.”
“It'd be a capital thing if he never turned up at all. Do you suppose I enjoy any of this, and in your company besides? So, we'll come to dinner. Thank the Father Superior,” he said to the monk.
“No, it's my duty now to take you to the elder,” the monk answered.
“If that's so, I'll go straight to the Father Superior—straight to the Father Superior,” babbled Maximov.
“The Father Superior is occupied just now. But as you like—” the monk hesitated.
“Impertinent old man!” Miüsov said aloud, while Maximov ran back toward the monastery.
“He's like von Sohn,” Fyodor Pavlovitch said suddenly.
“Is that all you can think of?… How on earth is he like von Sohn? Have you even seen von Sohn?”
“I've seen his portrait. It's not the features exactly, but something indefinable. He's a second von Sohn. I can always tell from the physiognomy.”

“Ah, I daresay you're a connoisseur in that line. But look here, Fyodor Pavlovitch, you said just now we'd given our word to behave. Remember it. I'd advise you to control yourself. If you start clowning I don't intend to be associated with you here… You see what kind of man he is”—he turned to the monk—“I'm afraid to be seen among decent people with him.” A faint smile, not without a certain slyness, crossed the monk's pale, bloodless lips, but he made no reply, and clearly kept silent out of a sense of his own dignity. Miüsov frowned more deeply than ever.
“Oh, devil take the lot of them—an outward show built up over centuries, and nothing underneath but charlatanism and nonsense,” flashed through Miüsov's mind.
“Here's the hermitage. We've arrived,” cried Fyodor Pavlovitch. “The gates are shut.”
And he crossed himself repeatedly before the saints painted above and along the sides of the gates.

“When in Rome, do as the Romans do. Here in this hermitage there are twenty-five saints saving their souls. They look each other over and eat cabbage. And not one woman sets foot through this gate. That's the remarkable thing. And it really is so. But I did hear the elder receives ladies,” he added suddenly to the monk.

“Women of the common people are here too now, lying in the portico, waiting. But for ladies of higher rank, two rooms have been built adjoining the portico, outside the walls—you can see the windows there—and the elder goes out to them by an inner passage when he's well enough. They always stay outside the walls. There's a lady from Kharkov, Madame Hohlakov, waiting there now with her sick daughter. He's probably promised to come out to her, though lately he's been so weak he's barely shown himself even to the common people.”

“So there are loopholes, after all, to slip out of the hermitage to the ladies. Don't imagine, holy father, that I mean any harm by it. But did you know that on Athos, not only are women's visits forbidden—no creature of the female sex is allowed at all, not hens, not turkey-hens, not cows.”
“Fyodor Pavlovitch, I warn you, I'll turn around and leave you here. They'll throw you out the moment I'm gone.”
“But I'm not bothering you, Pyotr Alexandrovitch. Look,” he cried suddenly, stepping inside the grounds, “what a vale of roses they live in!”

Though there were no roses at that season, there were plenty of rare, beautiful autumn flowers growing wherever there was room for them, clearly tended by a skilled hand; there were flower beds around the church and between the graves, and the one-story wooden house where the elder lived was likewise surrounded with flowers.

“And was it like this in the time of the last elder, Varsonofy? He had no use for that kind of elegance. They say he used to jump up and thrash even the ladies with a stick,” Fyodor Pavlovitch remarked, climbing the steps.

“The elder Varsonofy did sometimes seem rather strange, but a lot of what's said is nonsense. He never thrashed anyone,” the monk answered. “Now, gentlemen, if you'll wait a moment, I'll go announce you.”
“Fyodor Pavlovitch, for the last time—our agreement, do you hear? Behave yourself or I'll make you pay for it!” Miüsov managed to mutter again.

“I can't think why you're so worked up,” Fyodor Pavlovitch observed sarcastically. “Worried about your sins? They say he can tell what someone's come about just from their eyes. And what a lot of stock you put in their opinion, you—a Parisian, and so advanced! I'm amazed at you.”
But Miüsov had no time to answer this jab. They were asked to come in. He walked in, somewhat irritated.
“Now I know myself—I'm annoyed, I'll lose my temper and start a quarrel—and lower myself and my principles along with it,” he thought.
